en: The Sūtra on King Mādhava Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Song dynasty layman Juqu Jingsheng.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha together with twelve hundred [monks].
There were fifty bhikṣus with him.

At that time, there was a king named King Mada, who was about to dispatch an army for a military expedition; he selected several million people from within his kingdom, all of whom were required to go along as followers.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had already attained the path of arhatship; he went to that country for alms and was arrested, then led to the gate of the royal palace.
The king had a stable master who ordered the bhikṣu to tend to the official horses, which he did with diligent toil for seven days.

Later, when the king personally went to inspect the military formations, the bhikṣu saw the king and immediately rose up before him, flying lightly into the air to manifest his majestic spiritual power.
The king was immediately struck with terror; he bowed his head to the ground and repented, saying:
"I am truly foolish and failed to distinguish between the true and the false.
Let it be investigated within the realm who incited this divine person to act thus; they shall now be punished and executed."
The bhikṣu said to the king:
"This is not the fault of the king or the people of the country; it is due to my own past lives.
While practicing the Way, I always made offerings to my teacher. On one occasion, when I had prepared a meal for my teacher, the teacher said to me:"
"Furthermore, one must first wash one's hands before eating.
Being foolish, I thought to myself:
"The teacher does not even keep official horses; why then does he not wash his hands beforehand?"
The teacher then said to me:
"You think lightly of this now; how will it be when it becomes heavy later?
Upon hearing these words, I was filled with sorrow and anxiety.
The Master, perceiving his intention, thought to himself:
"I shall soon enter parinirvāṇa; why should I cause others such distress?
Thereupon, during the third watch of that very night, he entered parinirvāṇa.
From time immemorial, we have each undergone cycles of birth and death; it is for this reason that we now suffer the retribution of our past karma by tending horses for seven days.
Indeed, good and evil deeds invariably bring about calamity or fortune, just as a shadow follows a form.
When the king heard the bhikṣu speak of transgressions and blessings, his mind was awakened and he rejoiced; he requested permission to take refuge in the divine man.
The bhikṣu told him:
“You should take refuge in the Buddha yourself; the Buddha is the teacher of the three realms.”
The king and the people of the kingdom all followed the bhikṣu to the Buddha’s dwelling; they prostrated themselves before the Buddha in salutation, received the five precepts, and became upāsakas.

The Buddha then manifested his physical marks, signs of excellence, and majestic spiritual power for the king and the people, its radiance illuminating heaven and earth. He further preached to them on impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.

Thereupon, the king attained the stage of Srotāpanna, and all the people within the kingdom received the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions, took refuge in the Triple Gem, and observed the fasts on the first and fifteenth days of the month as their constant practice.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, paid homage, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This king and the people of the kingdom understand upon seeing the Buddha and hearing the sutra; for what reason is this?"
The Buddha said:

"In the past, during the time of the Buddha Maphu, this bhikṣu was a śramaṇa and the king was an upāsaka; for three days they made offerings with pure intent, whereby I have always received their merit wherever I dwell."
"Now that you have attained the Way of transcending the world, you have come to this assembly and, upon hearing this sutra, immediately realized the stage of Srotāpanna.
The fourfold assembly of disciples, as well as the devas, nāgas, and spirits, rejoiced upon hearing the sutra; they came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and departed.
The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on King Madaṭa.
